user_input: What's the recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it?
reference: Reach for a role locator such as page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }). Playwright pushes you toward role-based locators because they mirror how real users and assistive tech experience the page.
reference_contexts: We recommend prioritizing role locators to locate elements, as it is the closest way to how users and assistive technology perceive the page.

user_input: If I don't configure anything, how long can a single test run before Playwright kills it, and what counts toward that budget?
reference: Each test gets 30 seconds out of the box, and that budget covers the test body plus fixture setup and any beforeEach hooks.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.

user_input: How long does a web-first assertion like toHaveText keep retrying before giving up, if I leave the defaults?
reference: Web-first assertions retry for about 5 seconds by default, and that clock runs independently of the overall test timeout.
reference_contexts: Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout. It produces the following error:

user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.

user_input: How do I grab a screenshot of the whole scrollable page rather than just the visible area?
reference: Flip on the fullPage flag when you screenshot the page: page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true }).
reference_contexts: await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true });

user_input: Can I screenshot a single element instead of the entire page?
reference: Yes — call .screenshot() directly on that element's locator, e.g. page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' }).
reference_contexts: await page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' });

user_input: Do I get videos of my test runs automatically, or do I have to switch them on?
reference: They stay off unless you opt in; a single config setting — video — turns recording on and selects the mode.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the video option in your Playwright config. By default videos are off.

user_input: I pulled a trace.zip off CI — how do I actually open it on my machine?
reference: Hand it to the CLI: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip.
reference_contexts: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip

user_input: How can I cap how many tests run in parallel straight from the command line?
reference: Bound the parallel worker count with the --workers flag, e.g. npx playwright test --workers 4.
reference_contexts: npx playwright test --workers 4

user_input: If my selector happens to match several elements and I try to click, what does Playwright do?
reference: It refuses to guess — locators are strict, so any action that needs one element throws when the locator resolves to more than one.
reference_contexts: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:

user_input: Which attribute does getByTestId read by default, and can I point it at a different one?
reference: It keys off data-testid by default, but you can repoint it via testIdAttribute in the config (or selectors.setTestIdAttribute()).
reference_contexts: By default, page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id) will locate elements based on the data-testid attribute, but you can configure it in your test config or by calling selectors.setTestIdAttribute() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-selectors#selectors-set-test-id-attribute) .

user_input: What's the simplest call to enter text into a form field, and does it also cover textareas and contenteditable?
reference: locator.fill() is the go-to: it focuses the field and fires an input event, and it handles <input>, <textarea> and [contenteditable] alike.
reference_contexts: Using locator.fill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-fill) is the easiest way to fill out the form fields. It focuses the element and triggers an input event with the entered text. It works for <input> , <textarea> and [contenteditable] elements.

user_input: What's the cleanest way to tick a checkbox or pick a radio button?
reference: Use setChecked() (or check()); it handles standard checkbox and radio inputs as well as elements that expose a checkbox role.
reference_contexts: Using locator.setChecked() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-set-checked) is the easiest way to check and uncheck a checkbox or a radio button. This method can be used with input[type=checkbox] , input[type=radio] and [role=checkbox] elements.

user_input: How do I choose an option in a <select>, and can I pick several at once?
reference: Call selectOption() with the option's value or label; pass an array when you need multiple selected.
reference_contexts: Selects one or multiple options in the <select> element with locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option) . You can specify option value , or label to select. Multiple options can be selected.

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.

user_input: What's the pattern to trigger a file download and save it where I want?
reference: Arm the 'download' wait before the click (don't await it yet), click, await the download, then saveAs() using suggestedFilename().

user_input: Where should I keep saved login state, and how do I keep it out of version control?
reference: Stash it in a playwright/.auth directory and add that folder to .gitignore; tests then reuse the saved state to start already signed in.
reference_contexts: We recommend to create playwright/.auth directory and add it to your .gitignore . Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this playwright/.auth directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

user_input: How do I make my tests render the app in dark mode?
reference: Emulate the color scheme — set colorScheme to 'dark' (the choices are 'light' or 'dark') in use, either globally or per test.
reference_contexts: Emulate the users "colorScheme" . Supported values are 'light' and 'dark'. You can also emulate the media type with page.emulateMedia() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-emulate-media) .

user_input: How do I pin the browser to a specific GPS location for a test?
reference: Set geolocation coordinates in use and grant the 'geolocation' permission — e.g. geolocation: { longitude, latitude } together with permissions: ['geolocation'].
reference_contexts: Grant "geolocation" permissions and set geolocation to a specific area.

user_input: How do I interact with a button that's rendered inside an iframe?
reference: Step into the frame with frameLocator and then locate as usual — the getBy* methods exist on FrameLocator, so you can chain: page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click().

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4

user_input: One test is genuinely slow and keeps timing out — is there a one-liner to give just it more room?
reference: Call test.slow() inside it; that marks the test slow and triples its timeout.
reference_contexts: test.slow() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-slow) marks the test as slow and triples the test timeout.

user_input: Why do teams add data-testid attributes instead of leaning on text or role?
reference: Test ids survive copy and role changes, so those tests keep passing even when the UI wording shifts — the downside is they aren't user-facing.
reference_contexts: Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. QA's and developers should define explicit test ids and query them with page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id) . However testing by test ids is not user facing.

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).
reference_contexts:
// Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });

user_input: Is there a way to stop a test at a chosen line and poke around, instead of stepping through everything?
reference: Drop await page.pause() at that line and run in debug mode; the Inspector plays up to the pause and waits there when you hit Resume.
reference_contexts: Once you add a page.pause() call, run your tests in debug mode. Clicking the "Resume" button in the Inspector will run the test and only stop on the page.pause() .

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.
reference_contexts: Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id locators. If the generator finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient that uniquely identifies the target element.
The test generator can also generate a test while preserving authenticated state.

Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.

Run with --load-storage to consume the previously loaded storage from the auth.json. This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.
You can generate locators with the test generator.

user_input: How do I make every browser project sign in once up front and share that session, instead of logging in inside each test?
reference: Add a setup project that logs in and writes storageState, then declare it as a dependency of your browser projects and point each project's storageState at the saved file. Because the dependency runs first, the tests begin already authenticated.
reference_contexts: Create a new setup project in the config and declare it as a dependency (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects#dependencies) for all your testing projects. This project will always run and authenticate before all the tests. All testing projects should use the authenticated state as storageState .

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.

user_input: When I shard across CI jobs, how do workers, fullyParallel and retries interact to keep runs balanced and reliable?
reference: Inside each shard Playwright still runs worker processes; turning on fullyParallel shards at the individual-test level so each job gets an even slice rather than whole files. Keep retries enabled so that when a worker is torn down after a failure it simply restarts and re-runs the affected test.
reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.
If you enable retries , second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.

user_input: Should I use a globalSetup file or project dependencies for one-time setup, and why?
reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.
reference_contexts: If you're looking to do general network mocking, routing, and interception, please see the Network Guide first. Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.
To disable service workers, set testOptions.serviceWorkers to 'block'.

Only the Service Worker-owned request for the resource was routable via browserContext.route(); the Frame-owned events for data.json are not routeable, as they would not have even had the possibility to hit the external network since the Service Worker has a fetch handler registered.

await context.route('**', async route => { if (route.request().serviceWorker()) { // NB: calling route.request().frame() here would THROW await route.fulfill({ contentType: 'text/plain', status: 200, body: 'from sw', }); } else { await route.continue(); } });
Requests for updated Service Worker main script code currently cannot be routed.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.
reference_contexts: Ensure CI agent can run browsers: Use our Docker image in Linux agents or install your dependencies using the CLI.
# Install NPM packages npm ci # Install Playwright browsers and dependencies npx playwright install --with-deps
The Command line tools can be used to install all operating system dependencies in CI.

GitHub Actions support running jobs in a container by using the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful to not pollute the host environment with dependencies and to have a consistent environment for e.g. screenshots/visual regression testing across different operating systems.

user_input: Can I authenticate through API calls and then hand that session to a browser context?
reference: Yes. Storage state is portable between an API request context and a browser context, so you can log in via the API, export the storageState, and create a browser context seeded with those cookies — and each such context stays isolated from the others.
reference_contexts: Storage state is interchangeable between BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) and APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext) . You can use it to log in via API calls and then create a new context with cookies already there. The following code snippet retrieves state from an authenticated APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext) and creates a new BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) with that state.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and are completely isolated, even when running in a single browser. Playwright creates a context for each test, and provides a default Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page) in that context.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.
reference_contexts: Mock API requests: All the requests made by the page, including XHRs and fetch requests, can be tracked, modified and mocked.
await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const json = [{ name: 'Strawberry', id: 21 }]; await route.fulfill({ json }); });

await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const response = await route.fetch(); const json = await response.json(); json.push({ name: 'Loquat', id: 100 }); // Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body with the given JSON object. await route.fulfill({ response, json }); });

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.

user_input: One fixture is slow, but I don't want to inflate every test's timeout. How do fixture and test timeouts relate, and what's the fix?
reference: A fixture's setup counts against the test's clock, so a sluggish one can trip test timeouts. Hand that fixture its own longer timeout through the tuple option and leave the test's timeout tight.
reference_contexts: By default, fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures) shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures) ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout.
export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout
beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.

user_input: I'm adopting Page Object Models — how do I wire them so each test gets a ready-to-use page object without boilerplate?
reference: Wrap the POM in a fixture created with test.extend(): the fixture builds the page object (and can do setup/teardown around it), and any test just lists it as an argument. Fixtures are reusable across files, so every spec shares it.
reference_contexts: Page objects simplify authoring by creating a higher-level API which suits your application and simplify maintenance by capturing element selectors in one place and create reusable code to avoid repetition.
To create your own fixture, use test.extend() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-extend) to create a new test object that will include it.

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.

user_input: My manually-created context never produced a video file. How is video capture tied to the context lifecycle?
reference: Video is flushed when the browser context closes. With the test runner that happens automatically, but if you created the context yourself you must await context.close(), or the file won't be written.
reference_contexts: Videos are saved upon browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts) closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close) .
When using Playwright as a Test Runner, browser contexts are created by default. Otherwise, you can create browser contexts manually.

user_input: We rolled our own visual checks: capture a PNG, compare it byte-for-byte with a committed file, fail on any difference. It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. What does the built-in comparison do differently at each of those three points?
reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.
reference_contexts: Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

chromium-darwin - the browser name and the platform. Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms due to different rendering, fonts and more, so you will need different snapshots for them. If you use multiple projects in your configuration file, project name will be used instead of chromium.
Sometimes you need to update the reference screenshot, for example when the page has changed. Do this with the --update-snapshots flag. npx playwright test --update-snapshots
export default defineConfig({ expect: { toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixels: 100 }, }, });

user_input: In one test I need an admin and a regular user acting at the same time. How do I get two authenticated sessions side by side?
reference: Open two browser contexts in the same test, each seeded with a different storageState — one admin, one user — and drive their pages independently. Multiple contexts in one scenario is exactly how Playwright models multi-user features like chat, and they stay isolated.
reference_contexts: Use multiple BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s and Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page) s with different storage states in the same test.
Playwright can create multiple browser contexts within a single scenario. This is useful when you want to test for multi-user functionality, like a chat.

user_input: We added an automated accessibility scan to the suite and it's been green for months. This sprint a screen-reader user reported that our settings panel now reads its sections in the wrong order after a refactor that only moved markup around — and the scan didn't say a word about it. What class of problem is that scan actually able to catch, what would have caught the regression, and can both live in the same test?
reference: The scan and the regression are aimed at different things, which is why one sailed past the other. An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.
reference_contexts: The following examples rely on the @axe-core/playwright package which adds support for running the axe accessibility testing engine as part of your Playwright tests.

Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
Accessibility tests work just like any other Playwright test. You can either create separate test cases for them, or integrate accessibility scans and assertions into your existing test cases.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.
Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.

user_input: I need to assert that every row in our pricing table renders right-aligned, which isn't in the DOM anywhere — it's a computed style. Nothing on the locator exposes it, and my first attempt at reaching into the page came back with undefined for the threshold I was comparing against, even though it's a plain number defined right above the call.
reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.
reference_contexts: The code inside locator.evaluateAll() runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem'); const texts = await rows.evaluateAll( list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

user_input: How do I run the same suite across desktop and mobile devices with the right emulation each time?
reference: Define a project per device and spread a device descriptor into its use (e.g. devices['Pixel 5']). Projects let you run the same tests under different configurations, and each project applies its device's emulated parameters.
reference_contexts: By using projects you can run your tests in multiple browsers such as chromium, webkit and firefox as well as branded browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. Playwright can also run on emulated tablet and mobile devices.

Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

user_input: I want the same fixture to behave differently per project — say a default item that changes. How do option fixtures and projects combine?
reference: Declare an 'option' fixture with a default value, then override that value per project in the config's use block. The fixture reads the option, so each project drives its own behavior in a type-safe way.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.

user_input: How do I tag tests to run just those from the CLI, and also carve tests into subsets at the project level?
reference: Label tests with @-tokens and select them at runtime via --grep. For a more structural cut, group tests into separate projects and let each project's own filter — say a testMatch on the file name — decide what it runs.
reference_contexts: You can now run tests that have a particular tag with --grep (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli#all-options) command line option.

We can split tests into projects and use filters to run a subset of tests. For example, we can create a project that runs tests using a filter matching all tests with a specific file name. We can then have another group of tests that ignore specific test files.

user_input: I want to parameterize the same tests with different values — both at the test level and across environments. How do these two levels differ?
reference: You can parameterize at the test level or the project level. Project-level parameterization uses option fixtures whose values you set in each project's config, which is how you run the same tests against different environments.
reference_contexts: You can either parameterize tests on a test level or on a project level.

Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .

await page.locator('button').click();

Error:

Error: strict mode violation: locator('button') resolved to 2 elements

How do I click only the visible one?
reference: The locator matched both buttons and threw a strictness violation. Filter to only visible elements, e.g. await page.locator('button').filter({ visible: true }).click(); (or use the css :visible pseudo-class). Locators are strict and throw when more than one element matches.
reference_contexts: Consider a page with two buttons, the first invisible and the second visible (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#visible) .
This will find both buttons and throw a strictness (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#strictness) violation error:
This will only find a second button, because it is visible, and then click it.
await page.locator('button').filter({ visible: true }).click();

One spec in our checkout suite never finishes — the runner sits on it until the whole run is killed. It's the test that exercises the 'delete saved card' button, which is the only place in the app that asks the user to confirm before proceeding. I added a listener so I could log what the prompt says, and the message does get printed, so it's not that we're missing the event. reference: The dialog listener must actually handle the dialog by calling dialog.accept() or dialog.dismiss(); otherwise the action stalls because dialogs are modals that block page execution. Fix by accepting/dismissing, e.g. page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept()).

That's because dialogs in Web are modals and therefore block further page execution until they are handled.

A colleague added visual coverage to the checkout page and CI went red on the very first run of the new test — before anyone had changed any styling. The message doesn't read like a normal assertion failure and there's no diff image in the report, just this:

reference: No. On first execution there is no golden file yet, so Playwright takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match, saves the last as the reference, and reports this message. The generated snapshot is ready to be committed; subsequent runs compare against it.

Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

reference: The recording is only flushed when the context shuts down. Because you built the context yourself, you have to await context.close() for the file to land — until the page or context closes, nothing is available.

reference: :has-text() matches any element containing the text, so used alone it matches many elements including <body>. Combine it with another CSS specifier, e.g. await page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();

reference: networkidle is discouraged — there are always network connections (polling/analytics) so it never settles. Don't use it for testing; rely on web (auto-retrying) assertions to assess readiness, e.g. just await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Welcome' })).toBeVisible() and drop the networkidle wait.
reference_contexts: 'networkidle' - DISCOURAGED consider operation to be finished when there are no network connections for at least 500 ms. Don't use this method for testing, rely on web assertions to assess readiness instead.
Playwright includes auto-retrying assertions that remove flakiness by waiting until the condition is met, similarly to auto-waiting before actions.

reference: Mock Service Worker registers a service worker that grabs the traffic first, so Playwright's route() never sees it. Either set serviceWorkers to 'block' to remove that layer, or drop MSW and mock responses with Playwright's own routing.
reference_contexts: It might be that you are using a mock tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW). While this tool works out of the box for mocking responses, it adds its own Service Worker that takes over the network requests, hence making them invisible to browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) .

If you're using Playwright's native browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) , and it appears network events are missing, disable Service Workers by setting serviceWorkers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context-option-service-workers) to 'block' .

reference: Only targeted input actions (click, fill, inputValue, etc.) retarget from label to control. Other methods, like expect(locator).toHaveText(), target the label itself and assert the label's text content, not the input field. This behavior is expected.
reference_contexts: Targeted input actions in Playwright automatically distinguish between labels and controls, so you can target the label to perform an action on the associated control.

However, other methods will target the label itself, for example expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) will assert the text content of the label, not the input field.

// Fill the input by targeting the label.
await expect(page.locator('label')).toHaveText('Password');

Clear the session for that file with test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } }) so the test opts out of the project-wide logged-in state.

reference: Stop pointing per-test logins at the shared auth file. For state that shouldn't survive across runs, save it under the project's outputDir instead — that folder is wiped before each run — and drop any stored state once it has expired.

reference: Pages that depend on the dragover event need the pointer moved more than once for it to fire in every browser. Add a second move over the target: hover the source, press down, hover the target, hover it again, then release.
reference_contexts: If your page relies on the dragover event being dispatched, you need at least two mouse moves to trigger it in all browsers. To reliably issue the second mouse move, repeat your mouse.move() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-mouse#mouse-move) or locator.hover() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-hover) twice. My click fails because a hover overlay intercepts the click at the action point, even though I know the element is fine. Code:

await page.getByRole('button').click(); // fails actionability / receives-events

How can I bypass the check?
reference: Actionability checks include the element receiving pointer events; an overlay intercepting the click causes failure. If you know this is happening, bypass the checks with force: true, e.g. await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true }).
reference_contexts: Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability) checks and force the click:
await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });

Some actions like locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) support force option that disables non-essential actionability checks, for example passing truthy force to locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) method will not check that the target element actually receives click events.

reference: XPath is the one locator type that can't cross a shadow boundary. Every other Playwright locator reaches into open shadow DOM on its own (closed-mode roots aside), so switch to a text, role, or CSS locator such as page.getByText('Details').
reference_contexts: All locators in Playwright by default work with elements in Shadow DOM. The exceptions are:
Locating by XPath does not pierce shadow roots.

reference: Tests running in parallel live in separate worker processes with no shared memory, so a module-level variable in one is invisible to another, and workers can't message each other. Each runs its own hooks — design the tests to stand alone rather than passing data through globals.
reference_contexts: Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including beforeAll and afterAll .

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

reference: When any test fails, Playwright discards the entire worker process (and its browser) and starts a new one, continuing with the next test. The new worker re-runs beforeAll. This guarantees a pristine environment so failing tests can't affect healthy ones.
reference_contexts: Should any test fail , Playwright Test will discard the entire worker process along with the browser and will start a new one. Testing will continue in the new worker process starting with the next test.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

reference: Init scripts run before the page starts loading, so you must add them before navigating. Register the init script in a beforeEach (before goto), so it is evaluated in the page before it loads.
reference_contexts: Sometimes it is convenient to evaluate something in the page before it starts loading. For example, you might want to setup some mocks or test data.

Our submit-confirmation test fails maybe one run in ten on CI and never on my machine. When it fails the value read back is an empty string rather than the wrong string, so it looks like we're reading too early — but there's already a visibility check above this line, so the element is definitely on the page by the time we get here.

const text = await page.getByTestId('status').textContent();
expect(text).toBe('Submitted');  // sometimes empty

Adding a fixed wait makes it pass, which I know is the wrong answer. What's the right one?
reference: You're using a non-retrying check on asynchronously-updated content. Use a web-first auto-retrying assertion that waits until the condition is met, e.g. await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted'). It re-fetches and re-checks until it passes or the timeout is reached.
reference_contexts: Playwright also includes web-specific async matchers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions) that will wait until the expected condition is met. Consider the following example:
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');

Playwright will be re-testing the element with the test id of status until the fetched element has the "Submitted" text. It will re-fetch the element and check it over and over, until the condition is met or until the timeout is reached.

user_input: All my tests use the same test account and none of them change server-side data. I just want to log in once and have every test start authenticated, as fast as possible. What's the right setup?
reference: Go with the shared-account pattern that fits state-free suites: sign in a single time in a setup project, persist that session, and have every test start from it so none of them repeat the login.

user_input: Our app asks for permission to send notifications the moment the dashboard loads, and the browser prompt sits on top of everything so the test can never reach the page behind it. I want the tests to behave as though the user already agreed, without clicking through a native dialog.

Set `permissions: ['notifications']` under `use` in the config to grant it for every test, or pass it to browser.newContext({ permissions: ['notifications'] }) for a manually created context. If you only want it for a particular site, call context.grantPermissions(['notifications'], { origin: 'https://example.com' }) — a beforeEach hook is a convenient place, so each test's page starts with the permission already granted for that origin.

export default defineConfig({ use: { // Grants specified permissions to the browser context. permissions: ['notifications'], }, });
await context.grantPermissions(['notifications'], { origin: 'https://skype.com' });

user_input: My tests are slow because the page loads lots of images I don't care about. Can I stop images from loading to speed things up?
reference: Yes — abort image requests with routing. For example, block png/jpeg with await page.route(/(png|jpeg)$/, route => route.abort()); or abort by resource type using route.request().resourceType() === 'image'.

reference: Intercept the endpoint with page.route() and hand back your own payload via route.fulfill() before you navigate. The real API is never contacted — the page just renders your fixture data.
reference_contexts: The following code will intercept all the calls to */**/api/v1/fruits and will return a custom response instead. No requests to the API will be made. The test goes to the URL that uses the mocked route and asserts that mock data is present on the page.

user_input: I've configured many browser projects, but right now I just want to run my tests in Firefox only. How?
reference: Use the --project command line option to run a single project: npx playwright test --project=firefox. By default Playwright runs all projects.
reference_contexts: Use the --project command line option to run a single project.

npx playwright test --project=firefox

Running 1 test using 1 worker

  ✓ [firefox] › example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test (2s)

user_input: A test keeps flaking on CI and I can't reproduce it locally. I want a way to see exactly what happened when it failed, without slowing down the whole run. What should I enable?
reference: Enable tracing on the first retry (trace: 'on-first-retry' with retries enabled). This produces a trace.zip for retried tests that you can open in Trace Viewer to explore each action, DOM snapshots, console and network. Traces are great for debugging failures on CI.
reference_contexts: Traces are a great way for debugging your tests when they fail on CI. You can open traces locally or in your browser on trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev) .

Traces should be run on continuous integration on the first retry of a failed test by setting the trace: 'on-first-retry' option in the test configuration file. This will produce a trace.zip file for each test that was retried.

user_input: I want to run the exact same tests in two states — logged in and logged out — without duplicating the test code. What's a clean way to structure this?
reference: Reach for projects: they point the identical test files at more than one configuration — say one project with a signed-in storageState and one without — so you exercise both states without duplicating any test code.
reference_contexts: We use projects so we can run tests on different browsers and devices. Projects are configured in the playwright.config.ts file and once configured you can then run your tests on all projects or only on a specific project. You can also use projects to run the same tests in different configurations. For example, you can run the same tests in a logged-in and logged-out state.

user_input: I want a set of checks that talk to our backend directly — no browser involved at all — but I'd rather not stand up a second framework just for them. Ideally they run in the same command and land in the same report as the browser tests.
reference: You don't need a second framework. The test runner exposes a `request` fixture — an isolated APIRequestContext — that sends HTTP calls directly from Node without a browser, so you can write `test('...', async ({ request }) => { const res = await request.post('/api/issues', { data: {...} }); expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy(); })`. It honours the config's baseURL and other request options, uses the same expect assertions, and is collected by the same run and reporters as your UI specs. Requests do not run in page context, which is exactly why they're fast enough to use for setup as well as for asserting API behaviour.
reference_contexts: Playwright can be used to get access to the REST API of your application.
Sometimes you may want to send requests to the server directly from Node.js without loading a page and running js code in it.

test('should create a bug report', async ({ request }) => { const newIssue = await request.post(`/repos/${USER}/${REPO}/issues`, { data: { title: '[Bug] report 1', body: 'Bug description', } }); expect(newIssue.ok()).toBeTruthy(); });

user_input: Our dashboard greets people with 'Good morning' or 'Good evening' and stamps every row with a relative label like 'posted 3 hours ago'. The assertions on both pass when I run them at my desk and fail on the nightly build, which is obviously about when the run happens rather than the code. How do I make the page's idea of the current time deterministic?
reference: Pin the clock rather than trying to write assertions that hold at any hour. The recommended tool is page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')), which fixes what Date.now() and new Date() return so the greeting and the relative timestamps render the same way on every run. You can call it again mid-test to move to another fixed instant and re-assert. Reach for clock.install() only if the page's timers actually need time to progress — install is the heavier option that additionally lets you pauseAt, fastForward, runFor and resume — and setSystemTime is for advanced cases only.
reference_contexts: setFixedTime: Sets the fixed time for Date.now() and new Date().

The recommended approach is to use setFixedTime to set the time to a specific value. If that doesn't work for your use case, you can use install which allows you to pause time later on, fast forward it, tick it, etc. setSystemTime is only recommended for advanced use cases.
await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')); await page.goto('http://localhost:3333'); await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');

user_input: I want Playwright to launch my dev server before tests locally, but on CI I want it to fail if the server isn't already handled. Actually — I just want it to reuse an already-running server locally but always start fresh on CI. How?
reference: Set reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI in the webServer config. Locally it reuses an already-running dev server; on CI it will not reuse and starts the server fresh.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a webServer option in the config file which gives you the ability to launch a local dev server before running your tests. This is ideal for when writing your tests during development and when you don't have a staging or production url to test against.

webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start',
    url: 'http://localhost:3000',
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    stdout: 'ignore',
    stderr: 'pipe',
  },

user_input: Tests running on different parallel workers keep colliding on the same database user. I want each worker to use its own isolated user. What's the recommended approach?
reference: Use a worker-scoped fixture keyed on testInfo.workerIndex (or process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX) to create a unique DB user per worker, initialized once and cleaned up after. All tests run by that worker reuse the same user.
reference_contexts: You can leverage process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX or testInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-worker-index) mentioned above to isolate user data in the database between tests running on different workers. All tests run by the worker reuse the same user.

user_input: Our stack needs two processes up before anything can be tested — the web front end and a separate API service — and the API one is slow, usually a minute and a half before it answers. Right now the run gives up and everything fails at the first navigation. How should this be configured?
reference: The `webServer` option accepts an array, so declare both processes and let the runner wait for each one. Give each entry a `command`, a `url` to poll for readiness, a `name` so failures are attributable, and — for the slow one — a `timeout` big enough to cover the boot, e.g. `timeout: 120 * 1000`, since the default is not enough for a server that takes 90 seconds. Setting `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` on each keeps local iteration fast while forcing a fresh boot on CI. Pair it with `use: { baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000' }` so specs can navigate with relative paths.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a webServer option in the config file which gives you the ability to launch a local dev server before running your tests.
Webservers can sometimes take longer to boot up. In this case, you can increase the timeout to wait for the server to start.

webServer: [ { command: 'npm run start', url: 'http://localhost:3000', name: 'Frontend', timeout: 120 * 1000, reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, }, { command: 'npm run backend', url: 'http://localhost:3333', name: 'Backend', timeout: 120 * 1000, reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, } ]

user_input: My CSS selectors keep breaking every time the DOM changes. I want locators that survive refactors. What should I use instead?
reference: Prefer user-facing locators like role and text (getByRole, getByText) or an explicit test id contract (getByTestId) instead of CSS/XPath, which are tied to implementation and break when the DOM changes.
reference_contexts: CSS and XPath are not recommended as the DOM can often change leading to non resilient tests. Instead, try to come up with a locator that is close to how the user perceives the page such as role locators or define an explicit testing contract using test ids.
Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass.

user_input: I don't want videos for every test — only when a test fails. How do I configure that?
reference: Use video: 'retain-on-failure' — Playwright records every test, then throws the recordings away for the ones that passed, leaving only failures.
reference_contexts: 'retain-on-failure' - Record video for each test, but remove all videos from successful test runs.

user_input: I want a fast 'smoke' set that runs a small subset of tests with no retries, plus a default set that runs everything else with retries. How can I organize this?
reference: Split tests into projects with filters: a 'Smoke' project using testMatch to select smoke specs (retries 0), and a 'Default' project using testIgnore to exclude them (retries 2).
reference_contexts: We can split tests into projects and use filters to run a subset of tests. For example, we can create a project that runs tests using a filter matching all tests with a specific file name. We can then have another group of tests that ignore specific test files.

user_input: This particular feature isn't working in Firefox yet, so I want to skip the test only on Firefox but keep running it elsewhere. How?
reference: Use a conditional test.skip inside the test based on browserName, e.g. test.skip(browserName === 'firefox', 'Still working on it'). It skips only when the condition is truthy.
reference_contexts: You can skip certain test based on the condition.

user_input: One of my fixtures does a slow operation, but I don't want to bump the timeout for every test just because of it. What's the cleanest fix?
reference: Give the slow fixture its own larger timeout via the tuple notation ({ timeout: 60_000 }), keeping the overall test timeout small. A slow fixture otherwise counts toward the test timeout.
reference_contexts: Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

user_input: I keep writing teardown code to clear cookies and local storage so one spec doesn't poison the next, and it still isn't enough — things like already-visited link styling survive anyway, and a test that fails halfway never gets to its cleanup. I'd rather every test just began from nothing.
reference: That's the default, and cleaning up between tests is the strategy the docs advise against — it's easy to forget, and some state (visited links being the standard example) simply cannot be cleaned up, so leakage shows up later as a confusing failure in a different test. The alternative is to start from scratch, which is what browser contexts give you: each test gets its own BrowserContext, an incognito-like profile with its own cookies, local storage and session storage, created fresh for that test and completely isolated even when several run in one browser. With the test runner this happens automatically — the `page` and `context` fixtures in each test belong to a context created for it — so you can delete the teardown rather than fix it. Contexts are cheap and fast to create, so there's no cost argument for reusing one.
reference_contexts: Tests written with Playwright execute in isolated clean-slate environments called browser contexts. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContexts which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and are completely isolated, even when running in a single browser.

There are two different strategies when it comes to Test Isolation: start from scratch or cleanup in between. The problem with cleaning up in between tests is that it can be easy to forget to clean up and some things are impossible to clean up such as "visited links".
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.

user_input: The file input on my page is created dynamically when I click a button, so I don't have a stable input element to target. How do I upload a file?
reference: Handle the filechooser event: start waiting for 'filechooser' before clicking (no await), click the trigger, await the fileChooser, then call fileChooser.setFiles().

user_input: I set a geolocation for my test, but partway through I need to move the user to a different location. Can I change geolocation mid-test?
reference: Yes — call context.setGeolocation() mid-test to move the user. Just remember the change is context-wide: it affects every page in that context, not one page in isolation.
reference_contexts: Note you can only change geolocation for all pages in the context.

user_input: My app talks to the server over a WebSocket. I want to test it without a real server by faking the entire WebSocket communication. Is that possible?
reference: Yes — page.routeWebSocket() lets you take over the socket entirely: instead of reaching the real server, you answer the page's frames yourself in an onMessage handler with ws.send().
reference_contexts: The following code will intercept WebSocket connections and mock entire communication over the WebSocket, instead of connecting to the server. This example responds to a "request" with a "response" .

user_input: I run sharded tests as separate CI jobs and end up with a separate report per shard. I want one combined report at the end. What's the workflow?
reference: Use the blob reporter on CI, upload each shard's blob report as an artifact, then in a final job download all blob reports into one directory and run npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html to produce a single combined HTML report.
reference_contexts: In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.
To merge reports from multiple shards, put the blob report files into a single directory, for example all-blob-reports . Blob report names contain shard number, so they will not clash.
npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports

user_input: Before a UI test runs, I want to seed the server with a new issue via the API so it already exists when the browser loads the page. How should I approach this?
reference: Use APIRequestContext to establish preconditions: create the issue via an API request (e.g. apiContext.post(...)) before navigating, then load the page and assert it appears. This prepares server-side state before visiting the app.
reference_contexts: Sometimes you may want to send requests to the server directly from Node.js without loading a page and running js code in it.
The following test creates a new issue via API and then navigates to the list of all issues in the project to check that it appears at the top of the list.

user_input: We have three kinds of account — an administrator, an ordinary member, and a read-only auditor — and different spec files need to run as different ones. At the moment each file signs in through the form in a beforeEach, which is most of our runtime. None of these tests change server-side data, so sharing the accounts is fine.
reference: Sign each role in once up front and hand the specs the saved state. Write one setup file per role that logs in and saves to its own file — playwright/.auth/admin.json, member.json, auditor.json — and match them with a setup project (`{ name: 'setup', testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ }`). Then declare a testing project per role that sets `storageState` to the matching file and lists the setup project in `dependencies`, so authentication always runs first and every test in that project starts already signed in. Point each project's `testMatch`/`testDir` at the specs for that role. This is the recommended shape when you have more than one role but can reuse accounts across tests; per-worker accounts are only needed once tests start mutating shared server state.
reference_contexts: You have more than one role in your end to end tests, but you can reuse accounts across all tests.

This is the recommended approach for tests without server-side state. Authenticate once in the setup project, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

Create a new setup project in the config and declare it as a dependency for all your testing projects. This project will always run and authenticate before all the tests. All testing projects should use the authenticated state as storageState.
projects: [ { name: 'setup', testMatch: /.*\.setup\.ts/ }, { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'], storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json', }, dependencies: ['setup'], } ]
